title: Intermediates Adsorption Engineering of CO2 Electroreduction Reaction in Highly Selective Heterostructure Cu‐Based Electrocatalysts for CO Production
abstract: DOI: 10.1002/aenm.201901396 process can promote the development of power generation from clean and renewable energies, the cyclic utilization of carbon resource, and the reduction of CO2 emission.[2] Therefore, it is highly important to develop new electrocatalysts that will not only possess attractive catalytic activity but also operate high efficiency of CO2 conversion. Currently, Cu-based materials have proven more efficient for catalyzing the CO2 electroreduction by both computational and experimental studies.[3] Among them, Cu2O hybrid materials are widely recognized as better electrocatalysts for CO2 conversion.[4] However, conventional Cu-based materials have some limitation in their intrinsic activity and CO2 conversion efficiency.[5] One of the strategies for modifying and optimizing the electrocatalytic performances of electrocatalysts is surface engineering through heterostructure formation.[6] Heterostructure electrocatalysts have explicated that there usually exists an electronic interaction between two compounds, which leads to a synergistic hybrid catalyst system that could alter the charge distribution in the hybrid electrocatalyst and beneficial for optimizing intrinsic activity.[7] Furthermore, metal nanoparticles modification can be utilized to control the adsorption of COOH* intermediates and suppress the adsorption of hydroxyl (OH) species so as to improve the efficiency of CO2 conversion.[8] Despite the enhanced catalytic performance reported by this approach, further development of a simpler method for the design of nanohybrid electrocatalysts by combining the advantage of both heterostructure formation and metal nanoparticles modification is necessary. Although understanding the CO2 reduction mechanism is critical to the rational design of more advanced electrocatalysts, experimental research in this area is quite rare due to the extremely low signal of intermediate. It requires simultaneous characterizations of the catalysts under actual reaction conditions. In situ Raman analysis is powerful fingerprintingtype spectroscopy that can be used for investigation of trace chemical intermediates in electrochemical reaction with high sensitivity.[9] This makes it particularly suitable for CO2 electroreduction systems in aqueous media. The challenge in the artificial CO2 reduction to fuel is achieving high selective electrocatalysts. Here, a highly selective Cu2O/CuO heterostructure electrocatalyst is developed for CO2 electroreduction. The Cu2O/CuO nanowires modified by Ni nanoparticles exhibit superior catalytic performance with high faradic efficiency (95% for CO). Theoretical and experimental analyses show that the hybridization of Cu2O/CuO nanowires and Ni nanoparticles can not only adjust the d-band center of electrocatalysts to enhance the intrinsic catalytic activity but also improve the adsorption of COOH* intermediates and suppress the hydrogen evolution reaction to promote the CO conversion efficiency during CO2 reduction reaction. An in situ Raman spectroscopic study further confirms the existence of COOH* species and the engineering intermediates adsorption. This work offers new insights for facile designing of nonprecious transition metal compound heterostructure for CO2 reduction reaction through adjusting the reaction pathway.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 is a promising route to produce value-added chemicals under mild conditions.[1] This new
Adv. Energy Mater. 2019, 1901396
© 2019 WILEY-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, Weinheim1901396 (2 of 9)
In this work, we report metal nanoparticle-modified Cu2O/ CuO heterostructure nanowires via simple calcination and rapid galvanic replacement methods. The as-prepared Cu2O/ CuO@M nanowires (M = Ni, Fe, Co) serve as excellent CO2 reduction reaction electrocatalysts. Cu2O/CuO@Ni nanowires display attractive catalytic performance with high faradic efficiency (95% for CO), low onset overpotential, and small Tafel slope. Both theoretical and experimental analyses demonstrate that the hybridization of Cu2O/CuO nanowires and Ni nanoparticles could not only possess the benefit of adjusting the d-band center of electrocatalysts to enhance the intrinsic activity but also improve the adsorption of COOH* intermediates and suppress the hydrogen evolution reaction to promote the CO conversion efficiency. In situ Raman spectroscopic analysis was employed to further investigate the possible pathways and the adsorption of COOH* intermediates during the CO2 reduction reaction. This work provides information vital to achieving the rational design of more efficient electrode for CO2 electroreduction reaction.

sections.heading: 2.1. Synthesis and Characterization
sections.text:
The Cu2O/CuO@M nanowires (M = Ni, Fe, Co) were synthesized using a two-step procedure (Figure 1a). First, Cu2O/CuO nanowires were primarily grown on Cu foam through calcination (Figure S1, Supporting Information). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images confirmed the nanowire arrays morphology of the Cu2O/CuO with 200–300 nm diameter (Figure 1b) on the surface of Cu foam (Figure S2, Supporting Information). Motivated by the electronic interaction concept that occurs when transition metals hybridized with another transition metal compounds,[10] the Cu2O/CuO@M nanowires (M = Ni, Fe, Co) structures were achieved via a rapid galvanic replacement method in 5 min. Nanoparticles of Ni (Figure 1c), Fe (Figure S3, Supporting Information), and Co (Figure S4, Supporting Information) were uniformly distributed on Cu2O/ CuO nanowires. Compared with the smooth nanowire surface

of Cu2O/CuO (Figure 1b), the transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis in Figure 1d shows that the nanowires of Cu2O/CuO@Ni hybrid are characterized with nanoparticles. The presence of Cu2O phase in pristine Cu2O/CuO, Cu2O/ CuO@Co, Cu2O/Cu @Fe, and Cu2O/CuO@Ni nanowires was confirmed by X-ray diffraction (XRD) analyses (Figure S5, Supporting Information). The (110), (111), (200), (220), and (311) phases of Cu2O (JCPDS no. 34-1354) were identified by the XRD spectra for all the samples in Figure S5a in the Supporting Information. The enlarged XRD spectra in Figure S5b in the Supporting Information show the (200) and (−112) phases of CuO (JCPDS no. 45-0937), suggesting the heterostructure between Cu2O and CuO. In addition, the (110) phase of Cu2O shows an increase after metal coating, indicating that the loading of nanoparticles could improve the content of Cu2O.
However, the peaks of nanoparticles of Ni, Fe, or Co cannot be identified. High-resolution TEM (HRTEM) analysis in Figure 1e shows that the lattice fringes obtained from nanoparticles at the edge of the nanowire in Figure 1d correspond to (010) phases of hexagonal Ni (JCPDS no. 45-1047), which confirmed the formation of Ni nanoparticles on Cu2O/CuO nanowires. Furthermore, selected area electron diffraction (SAED) collected at interface of Cu2O/CuO and Ni layer in
Figure 1e revealed that the nanocomposite consist of Cu2O, CuO, and Ni with diffraction rings centered at (311) for Cu2O, (112) for CuO, and (010) and (110) for Ni (Figure 1f). It should be noted that CuO only appears on the inside of the nanowire, suggesting a Cu2O/CuO core–shell structure. Additionally, high-angle annular dark-field scanning TEM (HAADF-STEM) and elemental mapping in Figure 1g–j revealed the presence and distribution of the individual elements in the nanowire, with a higher concentration of Ni at the nanowire surface, further indicating that the coating of Ni nanoparticles on Cu2O/ CuO and successful formation of Cu2O/CuO@Ni hybrid.
The chemical composition was determined by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and Raman spectra. First, according to Ni 2p high-resolution XPS spectra of the samples, Cu2O/CuO sample is Ni-free, while that of Cu2O/CuO@ Ni hybrid is characterized with Ni peak as shown in Figure 2a. The Ni peak at 852.6 eV proved that Ni nanoparticles only composed of elemental Ni but no oxides and/or hydroxides of Ni were formed.[11] The Cu 2p XPS spectra of the samples are depicted in Figure 2b and Figure S6 in the Supporting Information. The peaks located at 933.1 and 932.7 eV can be attributed to Cu2+ 2p3/2 and Cu+ 2p3/2, respectively, revealing that the as-prepared nanowires are Cu2O/CuO heterostructures.[6b,12]

This Cu2O/CuO heterostructure was further confirmed by XPS and Raman spectra. The Cu LMM Auger spectra of the samples are plotted in Figure 2c. Among them, the peaks located at 916.5 and 917.6 eV were ascribed to Cu+ and Cu2+, respectively,[13] verifying the existence of Cu2O and CuO. These results are consistent with the Raman spectra in Figure 2d. The two peaks at 412 and 637 cm−1 and the other two peaks at 210 and 621 cm−1 are the Raman fingerprints of Cu+ and Cu2+, respectively.[14] The CuO were partially converted to Cu2O after metal nanoparticles modification. This could account for the increase of the (110) phase of Cu2O after metal coating according to the XRD spectra (Figure S5, Supporting Information). In addition, both the Cu+ 2p and Cu2O Raman fingerprints of the hybrids exhibited an increase after the loading of metal nanoparticles, and the content of Cu+ in Cu2O@Ni nanowires is higher than others.
Insight information on the electronic interaction between Cu2O/CuO heterostructure and metal nanoparticles were theoretically and experimentally investigated by density function theory (DFT) calculation and further XPS analysis. As depicted in Figure S7 in the Supporting Information, DFT calculations show that the interaction between the Cu2O/CuO heterostructure and metal nanoparticles could influence the charge densities on the individual catalysts. The NBO charge distributions of
Cu2O/CuO@M nanowires (M = Ni, Fe, Co) show that both Cu+ and Cu2+ positive charge decreases, and O negative charge as well compared to those of pristine Cu2O/CuO nanowires. This indicated that there exist strong electronic interactions between the Cu2O/CuO heterostructure and metal nanoparticles. Further information on the electronic interaction between the Cu2O/CuO heterostructure and Ni nanoparticles was experimentally observed by XPS in Figure 2b. Both the Cu+ 2p3/2 and 2p1/2 of the hybrids exhibited a negative shift of 0.8 eV when compared to that of Cu2O/CuO heterostructure suggesting changes in the electronic state and electronic interaction between Cu2O/CuO and Ni after integration with Ni particles.

sections.heading: 2.2. CO2 Electroreduction Catalytic Performance
sections.text:
The CO2 reduction catalytic performance of the electrocatalysts was performed using a three-electrode system in aqueous 0.5 m KHCO3 electrolyte. The LSV curves of Cu2O/CuO nanowires with different metal nanoparticles are shown in Figure 3a. During Ar purge, the current below −0.8 V can be ascribed to hydrogen evolution reaction, the major side reaction during CO2 reduction reaction. Under CO2 bubbling, however, a dramatic current increase is observed which indicates that the

CO2 reduction reaction occurs readily on the Cu2O/CuO@M nanowires (M = Ni, Fe, Co).
Further investigations on the production during CO2 reduction reaction were measured via gas chromatography (GC) in Figure S8 in the Supporting Information and hydrogen nuclear magnetic resonance (HNMR) in Figure S9 in the Supporting Information. The partial current density of CO [PCD (CO)] determined by gas chromatograph is shown in Figure 3b. The PCD (CO) of Cu2O/CuO@Ni is significantly superior to those of Cu2O/CuO, Cu2O/CuO@Co, and Cu2O/CuO@Fe, suggesting its highly catalytic kinetics. It can be observed from the Tafel plots in Figure 3c that the Tafel slope of Cu2O/CuO@Ni is 114 mV dec−1, which is obviously lower than those of Cu2O/ CuO (248 mV dec−1), Cu2O/CuO@Co (162 mV dec−1), and Cu2O/CuO@Fe (122 mV dec−1). Moreover, the turnover frequency (TOF) values of Cu2O/CuO@M nanowires (M = Ni, Fe, Co) at different potentials were also determined and the results shown in Figure S10 in the Supporting Information confirmed that the Ni nanoparticle-modified Cu2O/CuO achieved the largest TOF values than those of Cu2O/CuO, Cu2O/CuO@Co, and Cu2O/CuO@Fe, indicating that the Cu2O/CuO@Ni actually exhibited superior and excellent catalytic kinetics.
A series of potential electrolysis measurements (Figure S11, Supporting Information) were performed to investigate the potential dependence of the Cu2O/CuO@M nanowires (M = Ni, Fe, Co) on faradic efficiency (FE). As can be seen in Figure 3d, FECO of Cu2O/CuO@Ni nanowires was found to increase gradually with increasing potential, and reaching a maximum FECO of about 95% at −1.2 V versus RHE, then decreasing slightly after this potential. This high selectivity for CO is superior to the previously reported Cu-based samples (Table S1, Supporting Information). The FECO of Cu2O/ CuO, Cu2O/CuO@Co, and Cu2O/CuO@Fe exhibits a similar trend with increasing potential in Figure S12 in the Supporting Information. By comparing the FECO of all the electrocatalysts in Figure 3d and Figure S12 in the Supporting Information, it is worth to point out that the CO2 reduction reaction FECO performance of the Cu2O/CuO@Ni is also superior to that of Cu2O/CuO, Cu2O/CuO@Co, and Cu2O/CuO@Fe. The stability test was also conducted for both Cu2O/CuO and Cu2O/CuO@ Ni nanowires at −1.2 V versus RHE (Figure 3e) and the Cu2O/ CuO@Ni nanowires electrocatalyst exhibited excellent stability than Cu2O/CuO. After stability test, the LSV curve and XRD pattern of Cu2O/CuO@Ni nanowires are nearly the same with the initial one (Figure S13, Supporting Information), indicating that the catalyst can operate efficiently even at long-term electrolysis. This excellent stability can be attributed to the protective and synergistic effect of Ni nanoparticles on Cu oxides.

sections.heading: 2.3. Computational Analysis
sections.text:
To unveil the CO2 reduction reaction catalytic performance enhancement mechanism and gain more insight into the impact and interaction of metal particles decoration, DFT calculations have been conducted to support the experimental results. The projected density of states (PDOS) of Cu2O/ CuO@M heterostructure (M = Ni, Fe, Co) is depicted in Figure 4a and Figure S14 in the Supporting Information. The
density of states at Fermi energy level (Ef) of Cu2O/CuO@ Ni heterostructure is higher than those of Cu2O/CuO, Cu2O/ CuO@Co, and Cu2O/CuO@Fe, indicating higher metallicity of Cu2O/CuO@Ni heterostructure and availability of electrons for a given reaction.[15] Another important finding was that the d-band center (Ed, commonly defined as the central position of the d-orbitals) of Cu2O/CuO@Ni heterostructure is −1.44 eV, lower than that of others (Table S2, Supporting Information). It has been reported recently that the d-band center is a good descriptor of the metal–intermediates interaction.[16] The electronic filing of the antibonding orbits counts on the energy of the orbit relative to the Fermi level and the energy of antibonding orbits is higher than that of d-band. This finding indicates that the d-band of Cu2O/CuO@Ni is farther from Ef after loading of Ni nanoparticles on Cu2O/CuO heterostructure, and the antibonding energy states are decreased, meanwhile the interaction between intermediates and surface is suppressed. These results also suggest that Cu2O/CuO@Ni heterostructure should display better intrinsic activity by adjusting the d-band center.
Previous studies have shown that the main pathway for CO production is the adsorption of HCO3− and COOH* intermediates (Equations 1 and 2).[17]

To better understand the reason for the higher FECO of Cu2O/CuO@Ni heterostructure, the PDOS of s, p, d, and sum orbitals of Cu2O/CuO and Cu2O/CuO@Ni heterostructure and p orbitals of C atom in COOH* after COOH* adsorption are provided in Figure 4b. There are five harmonic s–d overlaps between the C-2s and Ni-3d states at energy levels from 5 to −15 eV in the surface of Cu2O/CuO@Ni heterostructure. Contrarily, there are only three harmonic overlaps for Cu2O/CuO, showing the strong interaction between the C in COOH* species and Ni atoms in the surface of Cu2O/CuO@Ni heterostructure.[17] This result demonstrates that the hybridization of Cu2O/CuO heterostructure and Ni nanoparticles could improve the adsorption of COOH* intermediates and suppress the hydrogen evolution reaction to promote the CO conversion efficiency during CO2 reduction reaction.
The contact angles of the samples in different electrolyte were obtained to study the adsorption of HCO3−. The contact angle of Cu2O/CuO@Ni heterostructure with 0.5 m KHCO3 is 70°, while that of Cu2O/CuO is 130°, indicating that Cu2O/ CuO@Ni heterostructure has more active sites and lower interfacial resistance to keep good contact with the electrolyte,[18] therefore prompting CO2 reduction reaction catalytic performance. The adsorption of water on the electrocatalysts is a vital criterion for hydrogen evolution reaction. In Figure 4c, the calculated adsorption free energy changes of H2O shows that Cu2O/CuO@Ni is less likely to absorb water, which is in agreement with the higher contact angle of Cu2O/CuO@Ni heterostructure with 0.5 m KOH.
To visualize the incorporation between the COOH* intermediate and catalysts, we calculated the electron density difference of Cu2O/CuO@Ni and Cu2O/CuO after COOH* adsorption.

The charge distributed around the Cu atom (Cu2O/ CuO) moved toward the C atom side (COOH*) after the introduction of Ni, indicating enhanced binding energy between the adsorbates and the Cu2O/CuO surface. These results, in turn, demonstrate that Cu2O/CuO@Ni heterostructure is more likely to accelerate the CO2 reduction reaction than hydrogen evolution reaction.

sections.heading: 2.4. In Situ Raman Spectroscopic Study
sections.text:
To identify possible reaction intermediates during the CO2 reduction reaction, in situ Raman measurements of Cu2O/ CuO@Ni electrocatalysts were conducted from −0.4 to −1.2 V versus RHE in 0.5 m KHCO3 solution (Figure 5a). Bands observed at 3350 cm−1 is attributed to the H–O–H bending of water molecules adsorbed on the electrode surface.[19] During the CO2 reduction reaction, there was no observable Raman signal in the range from 700 to 2000 cm−1 until the
onset potential at −0.5 V versus RHE, except for the peak at 1064 and 1640 cm−1, which belongs to the HCO3− band and COOH* band respectively.[20] 13C isotopic substitution measurement was carried out to confirm COOH* band at 1640 cm−1. As can be seen in Figure 5b, the Raman peak at 1640 cm−1 shifted to lower wavenumbers 1510 cm−1. The downshift can be ascribed to the isotopic effect,[21] which further verify the Raman peak at 1640 cm−1 belongs to COOH* band.
In order to investigate the reaction kinetics on the surface of Cu2O/CuO@Ni electrocatalyst, we plotted the peak intensity of 1640 cm−1 at −0.6 V versus RHE as a function of time (Figure 5c and Figure S15a, Supporting Information). The intensity of COOH* increases rapidly first, then approaches the maximum, and finally remains stable. It is worth noting that the CO2 electroreduction process on Cu2O/CuO@Ni can be fitted with a monoexponential function (Equation (3)) and the low residual suggests that the kinetic plot was well fit (Figure S15b, Supporting Information).

Figure 5a also exhibits the relationship between COOH* band and potential. As the potential decreased, the intensity of those two bands increased until −0.8 V versus RHE, after which it remained stable following a further potential decrease. According to electrochemical research, the Cu2O/ CuO@Ni electrode is saturated with the HCO3− species at first, and then the adsorbed HCO3− species can be further reduced to COOH* intermediate. These results suggest that COOH* species may exist and play a role in the CO2 reduction reaction. Meanwhile, in the in situ Raman measurements at Cu2O/CuO electrode (Figure S16, Supporting Information), we did not find the band around 1064 and 1640 cm−1, which
further indicated that the metal nanoparticles modification on the surface of Cu2O/CuO nanowire could tune the adsorption of COOH* intermediate.
We also investigated the electrochemical behaviors of other Cu2O/CuO@M heterostructures by in situ Raman analysis. As can be seen in Figure 5d, the intensity of the Raman band at 1064 and 1640 cm−1 decreased in the sequence Cu2O/CuO@Ni > Cu2O/CuO@Fe > Cu2O/CuO@Co > Cu2O/CuO. It was concluded that the COOH* intermediate is more likely adsorbed in the Cu2O/CuO@Ni heterostructure, which is in agreement with the CO2 reduction catalytic performance results. This result, in turn, indicates that the adsorption of COOH* intermediate can be controlled by the metal nanoparticles modification.

On the basis of in situ Raman spectroscopic study and DFT calculation results, we can confirm a possible pathway for the electroreduction of CO2 to CO on Cu2O/CuO@M catalysts (Figure 5e), which is proposed by Koper and coworkers.[22] HCO3− could first be chemisorbed on the surface of the electrode, then reduced to *COOH intermediates. This intermediate can then be subsequently reduced to adsorbed CO* species, and then results in the production of CO.

sections.heading: 3. Conclusion
sections.text: In conclusion, we have successfully developed a facile approach to design a Cu2O/CuO@M heterostructured nanowires (M = Ni, Fe, Co) as an efficient electrocatalyst for CO2 reduction reaction in aqueous electrolyte. The heterostructure electrocatalyst was produced via a two-step procedure which includes simple calcination and rapid galvanic replacement method. The as-prepared electrode, Cu2O/CuO@Ni nanowires exhibit superior catalytic performance (such as high faradic efficiency, low onset overpotential, and small Tafel slope) for CO2 reduction to CO. Both theoretical and experimental analyses reveal that the electronic interactions and synergistic effect between Ni nanoparticles and Cu2O/CuO nanowires are not only favorable for improving the intrinsic activity of hybrid but also change the reaction pathways. Such synergistic effect optimizes the adsorption of COOH* intermediates and makes the electrocatalyst accelerate CO2 reduction to CO rather than hydrogen evolution reaction. In situ Raman spectroscopic study further confirms the existence of COOH* species and the engineering intermediates adsorption. Such studies provide a useful way for improving the catalytic activity of CO2 reduction reaction by tuning the adsorption of COOH* intermediates.

sections.heading: 4. Experimental Section
sections.text:
Materials: Cu foam (0.5 mm thickness, 99.9% purity) was purchased from Shanghai Zhongwei New Materials Co., Ltd., and was cleaned ultrasonically in distilled water, ethanol, and distilled water again prior to use. Deuterium oxide (D2O, 99.9%) and dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, 99.99%) were purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Bio-Chem Technology Co., Ltd. Cobalt nitrate hexahydrate (Co(NO3)2 · 6H2O, 99%), iron nitrate nonahydrate (Fe(NO3)3 · 9H2O, 99%), nickel nitrate hexahydrate (Ni(NO3)2 · 6H2O, 99%), and ethanol (99.7%) were purchased from Guangzhou Chemical Reagent Factory. Potassium bicarbonate-13C (KH13CO3, 98 atom% 13C) was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich LLC. All chemicals were obtained and used without any further purification. Millipore water was used through all the experiments.
Synthesis of Cu2O/CuO@M Nanowires (M = Ni, Fe, Co): The Cu2O/ CuO@M nanowires (M = Ni, Fe, Co) grown on Cu foam were prepared as follows. In a typical synthesis, the Cu foam (4 cm × 6 cm) was annealed in air at 150 °C for 2 h under air atmosphere with a heating rate of 5 °C min−1. The furnace was allowed to cool to room temperature and the Cu2O/CuO nanowires were obtained. The as-prepared Cu2O/ CuO nanowires were immersed in Ni(NO3)2 aqueous solution (50 mL, 10 × 10−3 m) at 60 °C for 5 min. The resulting Cu2O/CuO@Ni nanowires were washed by DI water and ethanol several times and dried in the oven at 60 °C. To control the composition of Cu2O/CuO@M nanowires (M = Ni, Fe, Co), the Au precursors were replaced by Fe(NO3)3 and Co(NO3)2 for Cu2O/CuO@Fe and Cu2O/CuO@Co nanowires syntheses, respectively.
Characterization: The crystal structures were determined by X-ray diffraction (Shimadzu X-ray diffractometer 6000, Cu Kα radiation, Shimadzu, Tokyo, Japan) at a scan speed was 2° min−1. The field emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM, Quanta 400/INCA/ HKL) was used to analyze the morphologies of the samples. Detail morphology and elemental mapping analysis were carried out using a high-resolution TEM, high-angle annular dark-field scanning TEM, and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping analyses were performed using a JEOL ARM200F microscope (JEOL, Tokyo, Japan) with STEM aberration corrector operated at 200 KV. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (ESCALab250) was used to confirm the electronic interaction, composition, and chemical states of the elements in the samples. The contact angle between electrodes and electrolyte were tested in a contact-angle goniometer (DSA100, Kruss).
Catalytic Performance: The electrochemical measurements were performed in a three-electrode system on an electrochemical workstation (CHI760E) (Shanghai Chenhua). The samples prepared above were used directly as working electrodes in 0.5 m KHCO3 electrolyte. The working electrodes used for electrochemical tests were sealed with epoxy resin, leaving a square with 1 cm × 1 cm in the area for measuring. Ag/AgCl electrode was used as the reference electrode and Pt wire as the counter electrode. The chronopotentiometric measurements were carried out also in solution of KHCO3 (0.5 m) with vigorous stirring by a stir bar. The liquid products were quantified by NMR (Bruker advance III 400 MHz) spectroscopy, in which electrolyte (0.5 mL) was mixed with D2O (0.1 mL) and DMSO (0.05 µL) was added as an internal standard. The 1D 1H spectrum was measured with water suppression using a presaturation method. The evolved gas products were detected by gas chromatography (G5, Persee General Instrument Co., Ltd.). The turn over frequencies values for CO2 reduction to CO reaction were calculated using the following equation: TOF =  j ×  A/(z ×  F ×  n), where j is the current density at a given potential, A is the area of the electrode, z is the electron transfer number (2 for CO2 reduction to CO reaction), F is the faraday constant (96485 C mol−1), and n is the mole of electrochemical materials on electrode calculated from the mass and the molecular weight of the catalysts.
In situ Raman Characterization: A spectroelectrochemical cell with Pt wire and Ag/AgCl electrode serving as the counter and the reference electrodes respectively were used for the in situ spectroelectrochemical measurements. Raman spectra were recorded on a laser micro-Raman spectrometer (Renishaw inVia). The excitation wavelength was 632.8 nm from a He–Ne laser. The SERS spectra were obtained from at least 10 points to get the average information for each sample.
Computational Methodology: All DFT calculations were carried out with the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP).[23] 3D periodic boundary conditions were applied to simulate the infinitely large systems. A 20 Å vacuum space between sheets was set to prevent the interaction between two membrane layers. The Brillouin zone of the fiber was sampled by 1 × 3 × 1 k-points. The electronic structure of the system was treated using the generalized gradient approximation with the PBE functional.[24] The van der Waals interactions were added to the standard DFT description by Grimme’s D2 scheme.[25] In all calculations, the convergence parameters were 10−6 eV for the energy, 0.01 eV Å−1 for the forces, and an energy cut-off of 500 eV. A Gaussian smearing of 0.05 eV was applied. Charge analysis was performed via Bader analysis,[26] which included the core charges, and charge density difference analysis within VASP.
